# Simple TikZ Diagram

Here is a simple TikZ diagram without additional packages or complex features:

```{.tikz}
%%| filename: stick-figure
%%| caption: A Stick Figure

\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=2, transform shape]
  % Head
  \draw (0,0) circle (1cm);
  % Body
  \draw (0,-1) -- (0,-3);
  % Arms
  \draw (-1,-2) -- (0,-1) -- (1,-2);
  % Legs
  \draw (-1,-4) -- (0,-3) -- (1,-4);
\end{tikzpicture}
```


## All the features

Now, let's look at a more complex example [@fig-example] that uses additional packages and demonstrates more features.


::: {#fig-example .test-class}
```{.tikz}
%%| filename: my-fancy-diagram
%%| additionalPackages: \usepackage{adjustbox}

\usetikzlibrary{arrows, arrows.meta}
\tikzset{
  int/.style={
    draw,
    fill=blue!20,
    minimum size=2em,
    line width=0.5pt
  },
  init/.style={
    pin edge={to-, black, line width=1pt}
  },
  % Define a global path style
  every path/.style={
    line width=1pt,
    >=Latex
  }
}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
    scale=2,
    transform shape,
    node distance=2.5cm,
    auto,
    >=latex', % Arrowhead style
    line width=0.5pt % Base line width
  ]
  \node [int, pin={[init]above:$v_0$}] (a) {$\frac{1}{s}$};
  \node (b) [left of=a, node distance=2cm, coordinate] {a};
  \node [int, pin={[init]above:$p_0$}] at (0,0) (c)
    [right of=a] {$\frac{1}{s}$};
  \node [coordinate] (end) [right of=c, node distance=2cm]{};

  % Draw paths with arrows
  \path[->] (b) edge node {$a$} (a);
  \path[->] (a) edge node {$v$} (c);
  \draw[->] (c) edge node {$p$} (end);
\end{tikzpicture}

```

A fancy TikZ example
:::


## TikZJax (client-side) renderer

`%%| renderer: tikzjax` opts one block out of the local LaTeX run and hands
it to [TikZJax](https://github.com/artisticat1/obsidian-tikzjax), which draws
it in the reader's browser. The circle below is the only block here doing so;
the rest of the document still compiles locally.

```{.tikz}
%%| renderer: tikzjax
%%| caption: A circle, drawn by TikZJax in your browser

\begin{tikzpicture}
  \draw (0,0) circle (1cm);
  \draw (-1.2,0) -- (1.2,0);
  \draw (0,-1.2) -- (0,1.2);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Inline SVG (`embed: inline`)

`%%| embed: inline` puts the SVG into the page as markup rather than behind an
`<img>`. Try dragging across the triangle's labels below — then see the
[README](README.md) for why an `<img>` will not let you, and what
`svg-engine: dvisvgm` adds once you can.

```{.tikz}
%%| embed: inline
%%| alt: A labelled triangle
%%| caption: Inlined, so its labels are selectable text

\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.5]
  \coordinate [label=below left:$A$]  (a) at (0,0);
  \coordinate [label=below right:$B$] (b) at (2,0);
  \coordinate [label=above:$C$]       (c) at (1,1.5);
  \draw (a) -- (b) -- (c) -- cycle;
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## LaTeX passthrough

`latex-passthrough` hands the TikZ source to the host document rather than
compiling it to an image, so the diagram is typeset by the same LaTeX run as
the surrounding text — matching fonts and sizing for free, and producing no
figure files at all. It applies only when the output really is LaTeX, so
under this document's `format: html` the block below renders through the
normal SVG pipeline; render to `format: pdf` and the TikZ source is emitted
into the `.tex` instead.

Note that `\usetikzlibrary` is written in the block body as usual; the filter
quietly hoists it into the host preamble. The [README](README.md) explains why
it has to.

```{.tikz}
%%| latex-passthrough: true
%%| caption: Typeset by the host document under PDF output

\usetikzlibrary{arrows.meta}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.5]
  \draw[-{Stealth[length=3mm]}] (0,0) -- (2,0) node[midway, above] {$x$};
  \draw[-{Stealth[length=3mm]}] (0,0) -- (0,1.5) node[midway, left] {$y$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```
